title: Judge blocks Pentagon blacklist of Anthropic as supply chain risk
content:
A San Francisco federal judge on Thursday ruled that the Pentagon's blacklisting of artificial intelligence giant Anthropic earlier this year was illegal.
U.S. District Judge Rita Lin found that the Department of Defense violated the First Amendment by designating Anthropic a supply chain risk "based on a desire to make a public example" out of the company. Lin wrote that while the government is owed deference on matters of national security, its actions were not founded on any "articulable basis."
"Defendants claim that because of Anthropic's 'increasingly hostile manner through the press' and its criticism of the Department of War's views on AI use, Defendants 'cannot trust Anthropic to ensure the integrity of its models,' " Lin wrote in her order. "Neither the Constitution nor the federal statute invoked by Defendants allows them to impose sweeping penalties based principally on Anthropic's critique of the Administration's views."
In March, the DOD designated Anthropic a supply chain risk, meaning the company purportedly threatened U.S. national security, after negotiations about how the military could use its Claude AI models spiraled out of control.
Anthropic wanted assurance that its technology would not be used for fully autonomous weapons or domestic mass surveillance, and the DOD wanted Anthropic to grant the agency unfettered access to Claude across all lawful purposes.
Talks escalated and then collapsed, and Anthropic became the first American company to publicly be named a supply chain risk. The designation barred defense contractors from using Anthropic's technology in their work with the agency.
Anthropic sued the Trump administration in San Francisco and Washington, D.C., an effort to reverse its blacklisting. The DOD relied on two distinct designations to justify its supply chain risk action, which meant they had to be litigated in two separate courts.
Lin's ruling on Thursday handed Anthropic a major victory, but the company's litigation in D.C. is still ongoing. Until that case is resolved, Anthropic still technically remains a supply chain risk.
In a statement, Anthropic praised Lin's decision.
"We welcome the court's ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful," a spokesperson told CNBC. "We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology."
The ruling clears a significant hurdle for Anthropic as it marches toward what's expected to be a near-record IPO. While the company has shown no signs of a slowdown since the blacklisting, if it's able to reestablish ties with the Pentagon, it could open additional business opportunities that had been cut off.
Anthropic has said it brought the lawsuits an effort to return its business to the status quo before it was designated a supply chain risk. The suits would not require the Pentagon to restart its work with the company.

report.summary: Federal judge blocks Pentagon's blacklist of Anthropic as illegal, citing First Amendment violations over AI policy criticism.
report.background: Anthropic, creator of the Claude AI models, was designated a supply chain risk by the Department of Defense in March 2026. The designation followed collapsed negotiations over how the military could use Claude: Anthropic sought guarantees against fully autonomous weapons and domestic mass surveillance, while the Pentagon demanded unrestricted access for all lawful purposes. After talks spiraled, Anthropic became the first American company publicly blacklisted for supply chain risk, barring defense contractors from using its technology. Anthropic sued in two jurisdictions, and this San Francisco ruling found the Pentagon's action violated the First Amendment, saying the government made an example of Anthropic for criticizing administration views rather than proving an articulable national security basis.
key_points: Judge Rita Lin ruled the Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic was unconstitutional, finding the Department of Defense violated the First Amendment by punishing Anthropic for its public criticism of the administration's AI stance. The judge said no articulable basis justified the designation.

The dispute stems from a breakdown in negotiations: Anthropic demanded safeguards against fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance, while the Pentagon wanted unrestricted access to Claude for all lawful purposes. The collapse led to Anthropic's historic designation as the first U.S. company publicly blacklisted for supply chain risk.

Anthropic still technically remains a supply chain risk because a parallel lawsuit in Washington, D.C., remains unresolved. Until that case concludes, the blacklist status persists despite Thursday's major win in San Francisco.

The ruling removes a significant obstacle for Anthropic ahead of its expected near-record IPO. Reestablishing ties with the Pentagon could unlock business opportunities that were cut off, although the lawsuit does not require the Pentagon to resume working with Anthropic.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this ruling signals that national security designations cannot be used as a cudgel against companies that exercise free speech or refuse certain military applications. It sets a precedent that government procurement power has limits, potentially emboldening other AI firms to negotiate clearer ethical boundaries with defense agencies without fear of blacklisting. Developers at companies working with the military may gain more clarity on acceptable use cases, especially around autonomous weapons and surveillance. For users, the decision could mean broader availability of Anthropic's technology in defense-related research and infrastructure, while also raising the bar for how the government justifies security-related penalties.
report.tools: Watch Anthropic's Constitutional AI approach and Claude model cards for transparency expectations. Also monitor the Pentagon's Responsible AI toolkit and open-source projects like EleutherAI's evaluation harness for model safety benchmarks. For policy tracking, follow the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) publications on AI and national security.
